topic: Blog share: sleep is built, not owed
text:
After a bad night, the instinct is to sleep in. A new piece from psychologist Matthew Hallam looks at why that can make the next night harder.

Sleep is often talked about as a debt: miss some at night, pay it back in the morning. The two-process model offers another way to see it. A pressure to sleep builds from the moment someone gets up, and sleep at any time of day spends some of it. A sleep-in starts the build later, and a nap spends some of it early, so less is there at bedtime.

That does not make every sleep-in a mistake. A National Sleep Foundation expert panel agreed that regular sleep timing matters, and also that when weekday sleep falls short, catch-up sleep on days off may be beneficial. The useful question is whether someone is short on time for sleep, or short on sleep drive when they get there.

For anyone who talks with clients or patients about sleep: ask about the morning as well as the night. What time did they get up, and what did they do after a poor night?
